sentences.text: Terminocavus is recognized by a unique, heart-shaped upper frill that features a very narrow notch, setting it apart from close relatives like Pentaceratops and Anchiceratops.
This distinctive heart shape is formed by the parietal bone, which differs significantly from the anatomy seen in similar species.
The parietal bars of this animal are thin and extremely broad, appearing more like flat plates than the bars found in earlier relatives.
Six small horns, known as epiparietals, were arranged symmetrically along the parietal bone, with three on each side.
Evidence from the preserved right squamosal bone indicates that adults possessed a very large frill, comparable to those of their relatives.
Although its known remains are slightly smaller, Terminocavus reached an adult size roughly similar to that of Utahceratops and Pentaceratops.
The holotype presents a confusing mix of features, where the frill texture suggests a young subadult while the large size and fused horns indicate an adult.
The genus name means "reaching the end of the cavity," referring to the nearly closed parietal notch before it disappears completely in more advanced groups.
The holotype specimen was discovered in the Kirtland Formation of New Mexico in 1997 and was formally described in 2020.
It was found in grey siltstone deposits from the Campanian Hunter Wash Member of the Kirtland Formation within the San Juan Basin.
The species name sealeyi honors Paul Sealey, the individual who discovered the holotype specimen.
The holotype catalogue number NMMNH P-27468 consists of fused paired parietals, other skull fragments, a partial sacrum, and vertebral fragments.
It was informally named as a distinct genus in 2016 before being formally named and described by Denver W. Fowler and Elizabeth A. Freedman Fowler in 2020.
The specific name sealeyi refers to the discoverer of the holotype specimen, Paul Sealey.
The age of the specimen is undetermined; its frill texture suggests a young subadult, but its large size and epiparietal fusion indicate it represents an adult.
This contradiction between the texture of the frill and the size of the animal creates uncertainty about its exact life stage.
Terminocavus is classified as a member of the ceratopsid subfamily Chasmosaurinae.
Terminocavus was a member of the ceratopsid subfamily Chasmosaurinae.

Fowler and Freedman Fowler (2020) divide chasmosaurines into two lineages; a "Chasmosaurus line" leading to Kosmoceratops and a "Pentaceratops line" leading to more derived taxa, with Terminocavus belonging to the more derived line.
Phylogenetic analysis found Terminocavus to be relatively derived, more basal than Anchiceratops but more derived than Navajoceratops.
Terminocavus lived during the late Cretaceous Period in what is now North America.
Terminocavus sealeyi lived approximately 75 to 74.6 million years ago during the Campanian stage of the late Cretaceous in North America.
Terminocavus lived during the Campanian stage, from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
Researchers hypothesize that Terminocavus forms an anagenetic series with other chasmosaur species, representing a single population changing over time.
The phylogenetic tree for Terminocavus is considered unstable, as removing certain taxa causes the Pentaceratops lineage to collapse into an unresolved polytomy.
Joshua Fry questioned the assignment in a master's thesis in 2015, and a phylogenetic analysis failed to group it with other Pentaceratops samples.
